summary.text: A 54-year-old man with type II diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hypothyroidism, a prior left thalamic hemorrhagic stroke and poststroke seizure disorder, who had started carbamazepine for poststroke seizures, presented to the emergency department with an acute, progressively worsening generalized pruritic rash that spread from the abdomen and axillae to the limbs and face, intermittent fever and dyspnea at rest.

He was tachycardic, tachypneic and febrile, with generalized erythematous confluent rashes and non-follicular pustules. Admission tests showed leukocytosis with neutrophilia, glucose 881, pH 7.28, low bicarbonate, ketonuria, creatinine 3.0 and urea 172; blood culture was negative and chest X-ray and abdominal and pelvic ultrasonography were normal. Carbamazepine-induced AGEP with diabetic ketoacidosis was diagnosed; DRESS, SJS/TEN, generalized pustular psoriasis and sepsis-induced pustulosis were considered as differentials.

He was admitted to the ICU and treated with IV fluids and insulin infusion for DKA. Carbamazepine was stopped, with valproate and lorazepam substituted. Dexamethasone 8 mg IV stat then 4 mg IV twice daily was given for AGEP but complicated glucose control and was stopped, with topical steroid cream and an antihistamine continued. On the third day the infusions were stopped and a basal-bolus insulin regimen was used.

Cutaneous lesions improved from the third day of admission, and a EuroSCAR AGEP score of 9 confirmed carbamazepine-induced AGEP. Follow-up tests showed resolution of metabolic acidosis, normalized renal parameters and a lower leukocyte count. The rash resolved completely within 15 days of stopping the drug and DKA was successfully treated. At the follow-up visit the patient declined an advised patch test.

ambiguities.issue: The text places carbamazepine initiation 15 days before hospital presentation. The Figure 3 timeline prints a day-numbered axis whose carbamazepine-to-emergency-presentation interval differs from this; image values are recorded only in visual.json. The text itself is also arithmetically tight: the rash began about 13 days after starting the drug, the first febrile episode began with the rash and lasted about 4 days, and fever recurred 2 days before admission, which does not fit a 15-day interval.

ambiguities.issue: Dexamethasone is described as stopped because of rapid glucose fluctuation (b00050), while the discussion describes rapid tapering of systemic steroids once systemic and cutaneous symptoms stabilized (b00074). The two statements are compatible (a rapid taper ends in stopping) and are not a source conflict, but the source does not say whether the stop was abrupt or the end of a taper, nor which reason governed it.

article_limitations: Caption-layer visual status not_inspected; the four JPEG figures were inspected in the separate visual submission.
Day numbers printed inside Figures 2 and 3 are pixel content only (visual.json); the related text facts carry review_only ambiguities rather than conflict sides.
Table 1 group header rows (CBC, RFT, ABG, LFT, Urine R/M/E) are dashes without values and are not observations; panel names are not copied into method or specimen.
Table 2 histology cell is a dash and is recorded as not reported, not as zero or as the declined biopsy.
Reference ranges are recorded as printed; flags only from the table remarks or the case words, never from ranges. WBC keeps the printed scientific-notation text with no unit.
Author hypotheses on the mechanism of DKA, dapagliflozin role and atypical timing are not recorded as facts; literature cases (b00070) are not index-patient facts.
The systemic steroid ending is described as stopped (b00050) and as rapidly tapered (b00074); judged compatible rather than conflicting, recorded as an ambiguity with both facts included.

The text interval from carbamazepine initiation to presentation (15 days) is arithmetically inconsistent with the stated rash onset (about 13 days) plus the febrile course; recorded as an ambiguity only.
